perspective:
From Harold Padilla’s subjective perspective, he has access to:

- He is managing a project whose team appears unmotivated and behind schedule; he feels frustrated, anxious, and at his wit’s end.
- He had been focusing on project goals and deadlines rather than individual team members’ motivations.
- He met his friend Arthur Begum, a police officer he relies on for advice, at a coffee shop. Harold asked for advice about his unmotivated team.
- Arthur suggested understanding what drives each team member individually and having one-on-one conversations. Harold agreed to try this and felt more hopeful and relieved.
- Harold told his team he wanted one-on-one chats to learn what motivates them. One team member said it could be helpful; another said they were open to it. Harold said he would schedule time with each person.
- After implementing this, Harold observed the team still did not respond well. He felt disappointed and worried about the project’s future.
- Harold spoke with Arthur again. Arthur suggested there might be deeper issues—such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors—and that Harold might need to dig deeper.
- Harold decided to hold another round of one-on-one meetings to investigate team dynamics.
- In those meetings, one team member told Harold there was tension among some team members affecting work. Another team member told Harold they felt overwhelmed by the workload and stressed, making motivation hard. Harold said he would look into resolving conflicts and consider redistributing tasks.
- Harold then told the team he would create a more supportive environment with regular feedback sessions and team-building activities.
- Team members responded positively: one said it sounded great and helpful; another agreed and said it was good their concerns were being addressed.
- Harold felt optimistic and empowered, believed addressing individual concerns would improve team performance, and intended to work with the team to make the project a success.
